terms.definition: A number below zero, written with a minus sign, like −3.
terms.function: Models amounts below a zero reference — temperatures, debts, depths.
terms.whereItIs: The left half of the number line.
terms.whyItMatters: Negatives let math describe the world below zero.

terms.definition: The mark at zero separating positive (right) from negative (left) numbers.
terms.function: The reference point that every number is compared against.
terms.whereItIs: The central mark on the line.
terms.whyItMatters: Zero anchors all ordering — every negative is below it and every positive above it.

terms.definition: Arranging negative numbers by their distance from zero; farther left means smaller.
terms.function: −6 < −2 because −6 is further left of zero.
terms.whereItIs: Read directly from the number line positions.
terms.whyItMatters: It prevents the common mistake of treating −6 as bigger than −2.

terms.definition: Moving left on the number line by the size of the negative.
terms.whereItIs: The leftward stepping arrow on the line.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the rule that makes negative arithmetic consistent with the number line.

terms.definition: Moving right on the number line — the result becomes larger.
terms.function: 4 − (−2) = 6 because taking away a debt adds value.
terms.whereItIs: The rightward stepping arrow on the line.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the famously 'tricky' rule that trips students up — the line makes it visible.
